label: Problem set 13
title: Problem set 13: Double-layer structure and adsorption
summary: Practice with the double layer and adsorption: Debye length, compact-layer capacitance, adsorption isotherms, the point of zero charge and underpotential deposition.

intro.text: The double layer has a compact (Helmholtz) part and a diffuse (Gouy-Chapman) part; the Stern model combines them. The diffuse-layer thickness is the Debye length, about 0.304/sqrt(I) nm for a 1:1 electrolyte in water at 25 C.
Adsorption is described by isotherms: Langmuir for non-interacting sites, Frumkin when interactions matter. The compact-layer capacitance is C = eps0 epsr/d.

blocks.text: The double layer has a compact (Helmholtz) part and a diffuse (Gouy-Chapman) part; the Stern model combines them. The diffuse-layer thickness is the Debye length, about 0.304/sqrt(I) nm for a 1:1 electrolyte in water at 25 C.
Adsorption is described by isotherms: Langmuir for non-interacting sites, Frumkin when interactions matter. The compact-layer capacitance is C = eps0 epsr/d.

blocks.title: Debye length at low ionic strength

questions.question: At 25 C in water the Debye length is approximately 0.304/sqrt(I) nm for a 1:1 electrolyte, with I in mol/L. Calculate the Debye length in nm for I = 1.0e-3 mol/L.
Using the same relation, calculate the Debye length in nm for I = 0.10 mol/L.
questions.explanation: sqrt(0.10)=0.316; Debye length = 0.304/0.316 = 0.96 nm. Higher ionic strength compresses the diffuse layer.

questions.question: For a Langmuir isotherm the coverage is theta = KC/(1 + KC). Calculate theta for K = 1.0e4 M-1 and C = 1.0e-4 M.
questions.explanation: KC = 1.0e4 x 1.0e-4 = 1.0; theta = 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5, i.e. half a monolayer.

questions.question: The compact-layer capacitance is C = eps0 epsr/d. Calculate C in uF/cm2 for epsr = 6, d = 0.30 nm (3.0e-10 m), and eps0 = 8.854e-12 F/m. (1 F/m2 = 100 uF/cm2.)
In the Gouy-Chapman model the electrode is surrounded by:
options: A diffuse layer of mobile ions whose concentration decays into the bulk
A rigid layer of a single ion thickness only
questions.explanation: Gouy-Chapman describes a diffuse layer in which the counter-ion excess decays with distance into the bulk solution, in contrast to the rigid Helmholtz picture.

questions.question: The Debye length (thickness of the diffuse layer) decreases as the ionic strength increases.
questions.explanation: More ions screen the electrode charge more effectively, so the diffuse layer is compressed and the Debye length falls as 1/sqrt(I).

questions.question: The Stern model of the double layer combines:
options: A compact Helmholtz layer and a diffuse Gouy-Chapman layer
A single ion and a photon
questions.explanation: Stern combined the rigid Helmholtz layer of specifically adsorbed or oriented ions near the surface with the diffuse Gouy-Chapman region beyond it.

questions.question: The Langmuir isotherm assumes that adsorbed species do not interact with one another.
questions.explanation: Langmuir adsorption assumes equivalent, independent sites with no lateral interactions; the Frumkin isotherm adds an interaction term.

questions.question: Underpotential deposition (UPD) refers to:
options: Deposition of a metal monolayer at a potential positive of its bulk equilibrium potential
questions.explanation: UPD is the formation of an adsorbed metal monolayer at a potential less negative than bulk deposition, because the adsorbate binds more strongly to the substrate than to itself.

questions.question: Which factors affect the structure of the electrical double layer? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Ionic strength sets the diffuse-layer thickness, the electrode charge sets the field, and specific adsorption modifies the compact layer. Solvent colour is irrelevant to double-layer structure.

questions.question: The electrode potential at which the surface charge is zero is called the potential of zero charge. If the capacitance is 20 uF/cm2 near that point and the potential is 0.20 V from the pzc, what is the surface charge in uC/cm2? (sigma = C x E.)
Using Debye length = 0.304/sqrt(I) nm for a 1:1 electrolyte in water at 25 C, calculate the Debye length in nm for I = 0.010 mol/L.
For a Langmuir isotherm theta = KC/(1 + KC), calculate theta when KC = 9.
questions.explanation: theta = 9/(1 + 9) = 0.9, i.e. 90 percent of the sites are occupied.

questions.question: The potential of zero charge (pzc) is the potential at which:
options: The electrode surface has no net excess charge
questions.explanation: At the pzc the metal carries no net excess charge, the surface tension of an electrocapillary curve is maximal, and the double-layer structure is at its simplest.

questions.question: Specific adsorption of an ion generally shifts the potential of zero charge.
questions.explanation: An ion that adsorbs specifically on the electrode changes the interfacial charge balance and therefore shifts the pzc, often strongly for iodide and similar ions.

questions.question: Which statements about the double layer are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The compact layer forms within a few angstroms of the surface
The diffuse layer is several Debye lengths thick
Raising the ionic strength thins the diffuse layer
The double layer stores charge like a capacitor
questions.explanation: All four are correct: a compact inner layer, a diffuse outer region, compression of the diffuse layer by added electrolyte, and capacitor-like charge storage.
